When the combat to the death between Patroclus, who was wearing Achilles' armor, and Hector ended with Hector's victory, Alcimedonte took over Achilles' chariot, drawn by the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius, as he was described as an excellent charioteer.

Q3625035.label: Aventinus
Q3625035.description: mythological character son of Hercules and Rhea
Q3625035.lead: Aventinus was a son of Hercules and the priestess Rhea mentioned in Virgil's Aeneid, Book vii. 656, as an ally of Mezentius and enemy of Aeneas (Dryden's translation): Next Aventinus drives his chariot roundThe Latian plains, with palms and laurels crown'd.Proud of his steeds, he smokes along the field; His father's hydra fills his ample shield: A hundred serpents hiss about the brims; The son of Hercules he justly seems By his broad shoulders and gigantic limbs; Of heav'nly part, and part of earthly blood, A mortal woman mixing with a god.

Q3649829.label: Caieta
Q3649829.lead: In Roman mythology, Caieta was the wet-nurse of Aeneas. The Roman poet Vergil locates her grave on the bay at Gaeta, to which she also gives her name (cf.

Q3658204.label: Charaxus
Q3658204.lead: In Greek mythology, Charaxus was one of the Lapiths who attended the wedding of their king Pirithous and Hippodamia.

Q3664963.label: Cerambus
Q3664963.description: son of Eusirus in Greek mythology
Q3664963.lead: In Greek mythology, Cerambus, a son of Euseiros (himself son of Poseidon) and the nymph Eidothea of Othreis.

Q3676711.label: Cyllarus
Q3676711.lead: Cyllarus was a centaur in Greek mythology.

Q3684005.label: Combe
Q3684005.description: minor Greek river divinity, daughter of Asopus
Q3684005.lead: In Greek mythology, Combe was a daughter of the river god Asopus.

Q368994.label: Aglauros
Q368994.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Actaeus

Q3696513.label: Crantor
Q3696513.lead: In Greek mythology, Crantor was a son of Amyntor and possibly Hippodamia or Cleobule. He was probably the brother of Astydameia and Phoenix.

Q3698271.label: Crocus
Q3698271.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Crocus is a mortal young man who was changed by the gods into a saffron flower. Depending on the version, Crocus was the lover of either the nymph Smilax or the god Hermes.

Q3698712.label: Croton
Q3698712.description: son of Phaeax in Greek mythology

Q37340.label: Apollo
Q37340.description: god in Greek and later Roman mythology
Q37340.lead: Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology. His numerous functions include light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery.

Q374275.label: Anius
Q374275.lead: In Greek mythology, Anius was a king of Delos and priest of Apollo.

Q374311.label: Vertumnus
Q374311.description: In Roman mythology, is the god of seasons, change and plant growth, as well as gardens and fruit trees
Q374311.lead: In Roman mythology, Vertumnus is the god of seasons, change, and plant growth, as well as gardens and fruit trees. He could change his form at will; using this power, according to Ovid's Metamorphoses (xiv), he tricked Pomona into talking to him by disguising himself as an old woman and gaining entry to her orchard, then using a narrative warning of the dangers of rejecting a suitor (the embedded tale of Iphis and Anaxarete) to seduce her.

Q381459.label: Agave
Q381459.description: daughter of Cadmus in Greek mythology
Q381459.lead: In Greek mythology, Agave, was the daughter of Cadmus and a princess of Thebes. She is most well known for her role in the myths surrounding her nephew, Dionysus, god of wine.

Q385397.label: Glaucus
Q385397.lead: In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a Greek prophetic sea-god, born mortal and turned immortal upon eating a magical herb. It was believed that he came to the rescue of sailors and fishermen in storms, having earlier earned a living from the sea himself.

Q3899862.label: Periclymenus
Q3899862.description: son of Neleus in Greek mythology

Q391070.label: Hylonome
Q391070.lead: Hylonome was a female centaur in Greek mythology.

Q391091.label: Pentheus
Q391091.description: mythical king of Thebes, son of Echion and Agave
Q391091.lead: In Greek mythology, Pentheus was a king of Thebes. His father was Echion, the wisest of the Spartoi.

Q391379.label: Achelous
Q391379.lead: Achelous (also Acheloos or Acheloios) was the god in ancient Greek religion and mythology associated with the Achelous River, the largest river in Greece. According to Hesiod, he was the son of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q392631.label: Agenor
Q392631.description: mythical Phoenician king, father of Cadmus
Q392631.lead: Agenor was in Greek mythology and history a Phoenician king of Tyre or Sidon. The Greek historian Herodotus (c.

Q3954.label: Neptune
Q3954.description: Roman god of water, particularly the sea, considered equivalent to the Greek Poseidon
Q3954.lead: Neptune is the god of freshwater and the sea in the Roman religion. He is the counterpart of the Greek god Poseidon.

Q3991817.label: Tisiphone
Q3991817.description: ancient Greek mythological punisher of murder
Q3991817.lead: Tisiphone, or Tilphousia, is one of the three Erinyes or Furies in classical mythology. Her sisters are Alecto and Megaera.

Q4009778.label: Venulus
Q4009778.lead: Venulus was an ambassador sent by Turnus of Ardea to the Greek hero Diomedes to request assistance in a war against Aeneas. He appears as a character in Vergil's Aeneid (in Books 8 and 11, where he was killed by Tarchon) and Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book 14); in both epics, he seems to serve as a proxy or counterpart of the goddess Venus (Paschalis 288, Barchiesi 119), whose name is incorporated in his own.

Q404275.label: Acestes
Q404275.lead: In Roman mythology, Acestes or Egestes was the son of the Sicilian river-god Crinisus by a Dardanian or Trojan woman named Egesta or Segesta. According to Servius, this woman Egesta or Segesta was sent by her father, Hippotes or Ipsostratus, to Sicily, that she might not be devoured by the monsters which infested the territory of Troy and which had been sent into the land, because the Trojans had refused to reward Poseidon and Apollo for having built the walls of their city.

Q41054.label: Epimetheus
Q41054.lead: In Greek mythology, Epimetheus is the brother of Prometheus, with the complementary pair serving as archetypal representations of mankind. Both are sons of the Titan Iapetus; while Prometheus ("forethought, or foresight") is portrayed as ingeniously clever, Epimetheus ("afterthought, or hindsight") is considered inept and foolish.

Q4137657.label: Hesione
Q4137657.description: Greek mythical character, daughter of Laomedon
Q4137657.lead: In Greek mythology, Hesione was a Trojan princess.

Q416384.label: Acastus
Q416384.lead: Acastus is a character in Greek mythology. He sailed with Jason and the Argonauts, and participated in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q41746.label: Achilles
Q41746.description: Greek mythological hero of the Trojan War
Q41746.lead: In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus (Ancient Greek: Ἀχιλλεύς, romanized: Achilleús) was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.

Q419156.label: Acis
Q419156.lead: Acis and Galatea are characters from Greek mythology later associated together in Ovid's Metamorphoses. The episode tells of the love between the mortal Acis and the Nereid (sea-nymph) Galatea; when the jealous Cyclops Polyphemus kills Acis, Galatea transforms her lover into an immortal river spirit.

Q42603.label: priest
Q42603.description: person who consecrates his life to some divinity and whose main functions are to direct religious rites and offer sacrifices to the divinity (for a minister use Q1423891)
Q42603.lead: A priest is a religious leader authorized to perform the sacred rituals of a religion, especially as a mediatory agent between humans and one or more deities. They also have the authority or power to administer religious rites; in particular, rites of sacrifice to, and propitiation of, a deity or deities.

Q430157.label: Eryx
Q430157.description: in Greek mythology, king of the city Eryx in Sicily

Q44204.label: Cronus
Q44204.description: ruler of the Titans in Greek mythology
Q44204.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Cronus, Cronos, or Kronos was the leader and youngest of the Titans, the children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Cronus castrated and overthrew his father and then ruled during the mythological Golden Age until he himself was overthrown by his son, Zeus, and imprisoned in Tartarus.

Q45967.label: Persephone
Q45967.description: Greek goddess of the seasons and the queen of the underworld; married with Hades
Q45967.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter. She became the queen of the underworld after her abduction by her uncle Hades, the king of the underworld, who later took her into marriage.

Q463107.label: Autolycus
Q463107.description: son of Daedalion in Greek mythology
Q463107.lead: In Greek mythology, Autolycus was a robber who had the power to metamorphose or make invisible the things he stole. He had his residence on Mount Parnassus and was renowned among men for his cunning and oaths.

Q463865.label: Pleione
Q463865.lead: Pleione was an Oceanid nymph in Greek mythology and mother of the Pleiades. Pleione presided over the multiplication of the flocks, fitting, since the meaning of her name is: "to increase in number" (from the Greek word pleiôn πλεῖων "more").

Q4640.label: Vulcan
Q4640.description: god of both beneficial and hindering fire
Q4640.lead: Vulcan is the god of fire including the fire of volcanoes, deserts, metalworking and the forge in ancient Roman religion and myth. He is often depicted with a blacksmith's hammer.

Q464091.label: Silenus
Q464091.description: figure in Greek mythology; tutor to Dionysus
Q464091.lead: In Greek mythology, Silenus was a companion and tutor to the wine god Dionysus. He is typically older than the satyrs of the Dionysian retinue (thiasos), and sometimes considerably older, in which case he may be referred to as a Papposilenus.

Q46475617.label: Olenus
Q46475617.description: Greek mythical character, husband to Lethaea

Q4649.label: Jupiter
Q4649.description: chief deity of Roman state religion
Q4649.lead: In ancient Roman religion and mythology, Jupiter, also known as Jove (nom. and gen.

Q46491.label: Osiris
Q46491.description: god of the afterlife in Egyptian mythology
Q46491.lead: Osiris (from Egyptian wsjr) was the god of fertility, agriculture, the afterlife, the dead, resurrection, life, and vegetation in ancient Egyptian religion. He was classically depicted with a pharaoh's beard, partially mummy-wrapped at the legs, wearing a distinctive atef crown and holding a symbolic crook and flail.

Q466830.label: Myrmidons
Q466830.lead: In Greek mythology, the Myrmidons or Myrmidones were an ancient Thessalian tribe. In Homer's Iliad, the Myrmidons are the Achaean soldiers commanded by Achilles.

Q466866.label: Nessus
Q466866.lead: In Greek mythology, Nessus was a famous centaur who was killed by Heracles, and whose poisoned blood in turn killed Heracles. He was the son of Centauros.

Q467515.label: Zephyrus
Q467515.description: Greek god of the wind from the west, spring, fertility, procreation, luck, rebirth, vegetation, flowers, bees and honey
Q467515.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Zephyrus, also spelled in English as Zephyr, is the god and personification of the West wind, one of the several wind gods, the Anemoi. The son of Eos (the goddess of the dawn) and Astraeus, Zephyrus is the most gentle and favourable of the winds, associated with flowers, springtime and even procreation.

Q47231.label: Odysseus
Q47231.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Odysseus, also known by the Latin variant Ulysses (UK also ; Latin: Ulysses, Ulixes), is a legendary Greek king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer's epic poem, the Odyssey. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's Iliad and other works in that same epic cycle.

Q4749481.label: Amycus
Q4749481.lead: In Greek mythology, Amycus or Amykos was a male centaur and the son of Ophion.

Q47534.label: Anubis
Q47534.description: Egyptian deity of mummification and the afterlife, usually depicted as a man with a canine head
Q47534.lead: Anubis, also known as Inpu, Inpw, Jnpw, or Anpu in Ancient Egyptian (Coptic: ⲁⲛⲟⲩⲡ, romanized: Anoup), is the god of funerary rites, protector of graves, and guide to the underworld in ancient Egyptian religion, usually depicted as a canine or a man with a canine head. Like many ancient Egyptian deities, Anubis assumed different roles in various contexts.

Q47652.label: Venus
Q47652.description: Roman goddess of love, sexuality, procreation and pleasure
Q47652.lead: Venus is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory. In Roman mythology, she was the ancestor of the Roman people through her son, Aeneas, who survived the fall of Troy and fled to Italy.

Q488621.label: Anaxarete
Q488621.lead: In Greek mythology, Anaxarete was a princess from Cyprus, who is said to have been descended from Teucer. She attracts the love of a young man named Iphis, who she scornfully rebuffs, pushing him to the point of killing himself upon her doorstep.

Q492938.label: Mopsus
Q492938.description: seer in Greek mythology, son of Ampyx
Q492938.lead: In Greek mythology, Mopsus, was the Lapith son of Ampyx and a nymph (sometimes named as Chloris and sometimes named Aregonis), born at Titaressa in Thessaly, was also a seer and augur. In Thessaly the place name Mopsion recalled his own.

Q500739.label: Cecrops I
Q500739.lead: Cecrops was a legendary king of Attica which derived from him its name Cecropia, according to the Parian Chronicle having previously borne the name of Acte or Actice (from Actaeus). He was the founder and the first king of Athens itself though preceded in the region by the earth-born king Actaeus of Attica.

Q5011.label: Cupid
Q5011.lead: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. He is often portrayed as the son of the love goddess Venus and the god of war Mars.

Q501667.label: Lycaon
Q501667.description: Greek mythical character, king of Arcadia, son of Pelasgus and Meliboea
Q501667.lead: In Greek mythology, Lycaon was a king of Arcadia who, in the most popular version of the myth, killed and cooked his son Nyctimus and served him to Zeus, to see whether the god was sufficiently all-knowing to recognize human flesh. Disgusted, Zeus transformed Lycaon into a wolf, while Nyctimus was restored to life.

Q506781.label: Memnon
Q506781.description: mythical Ethiopian king, son of Tithonus and Eos
Q506781.lead: In Greek mythology, Memnon was a king of Aethiopia and son of Tithonus and Eos. During the Trojan War, he brought an army to Troy's defense and killed Antilochus, Nestor's son, during a fierce battle.

Q5089.label: Ganges
Q5089.lead: The Ganges is a trans-boundary river of Asia which flows through India and Bangladesh. The 2,525-kilometre-long (1,569 mi) river rises in the western Himalayas in the Indian state of Uttarakhand.

Q5113806.label: Chromis
Q5113806.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Chromis may refer to: Chromis, one of the centaurs who attended Pirithous's and Hippodameia's wedding and fought in the battle against the Lapiths. He was eventually killed by the groom.

Q512388.label: Androgeus
Q512388.lead: In Greek mythology, Androgeus or Androgeos was a Cretan prince as the son of King Minos.

Q53606.label: Philammon
Q53606.description: musician son of Apollo in Greek mythology
Q53606.lead: In Greek mythology, Philammon was an excellent musician, a talent he received from his father, Apollo.

Q54230.label: Nereids
Q54230.description: sea nymphs in Greek mythology, daughters of Nereus
Q54230.lead: In Greek mythology, the Nereids or Nereides are sea nymphs (female spirits of sea waters), the 50 daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris, sisters to their brother Nerites.

Q548099.label: Eurynome
Q548099.lead: In Greek mythology Eurynome was an Oceanid and the mother of the Charites by Zeus.

Q5623747.label: Psamathe
Q5623747.lead: In Greek mythology, Psamathe is a Nereid, one of the fifty daughters of the sea god Nereus and the Oceanid Doris. By Aeacus, the king of Aegina, she is the mother of a son, Phocus.

Q568768.label: Erigone
Q568768.description: daughter of Icarius of Athens in Greek mythology
Q568768.lead: In Greek mythology, Erigone was the daughter of Icarius of Athens.

Q575455.label: Antigone
Q575455.description: daughter of Eurytion in Greek mythology
Q575455.lead: The Greek mythological character of Antigone, was a Phthian princess who was the daughter of Eurytion, and the wife of Peleus. The meaning of the name is, as in the case of the masculine equivalent Antigonus, "worthy of one's parents" or "in place of one's parents".

Q578888.label: Ceyx
Q578888.description: mythical son of Phosporus, husband of Alcyone
Q578888.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcyone (or dubiously Halcyone) and Ceyx (Ancient Greek: Κήυξ, romanized: Kḗux) were a wife and husband who incurred the wrath of the god Zeus for their romantic hubris.

Q582268.label: Egeria
Q582268.description: legendary wife of Roman king Numa and minor goddess
Q582268.lead: Egeria was a nymph attributed a legendary role in the early history of Rome as a divine consort and counselor of Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome (r. 715 – 672 BC), to whom she imparted laws and rituals pertaining to ancient Roman religion. Her name has become an eponym for a female advisor or counselor.

Q59697.label: Hesperus
Q59697.description: personification of the planet Venus or its manifestation in the evening
Q59697.lead: In Greek mythology, Hesperus is the Evening Star, the planet Venus in the evening. A son of the dawn goddess Eos (Roman Aurora), he is the half-brother of her other son, Phosphorus (also called Eosphorus; the "Morning Star").

Q599489.label: Euphorbus
Q599489.lead: In Greek mythology, Euphorbus was a Trojan hero during the Trojan War.

Q599737.label: Marsyas
Q599737.lead: In Greek mythology, the satyr Marsyas is a central figure in two stories involving music: in one, he picked up the double oboe (aulos) that had been abandoned by Athena and played it; in the other, he challenged Apollo to a contest of music and lost his hide and life. Literary sources from antiquity often emphasize the hubris of Marsyas and the justice of his punishment.

Q6019476.label: Furies
Q6019476.description: vengeful deities of the Roman mythology

Q604898.label: Lucina
Q604898.lead: In ancient Roman religion, Lucina was a title or epithet given to the goddess Juno, and sometimes to Diana, in their roles as goddesses of childbirth who safeguarded the lives of women in labor. The title lucina (from the Latin lux, lucis, "light") links both Juno and Diana to the light of the Moon, the cycles of which were used to track female fertility as well as measure the duration of a pregnancy.

Q606422.label: Arcas
Q606422.description: son of Callisto in Greek mythology
Q606422.lead: In Greek mythology, Arcas was a hunter who became king of Arcadia. He was remembered for having taught people the arts of weaving and baking bread and for spreading agriculture to Arcadia.

Q60794133.label: Idas
Q60794133.lead: In Greek mythology, Idas may refer to the following individuals: Idas, son of Aphareus Idas, one of the Dactyls.

Q608951.label: Perdix
Q608951.lead: Perdix was, in some sources, a nephew and student of Daedalus in Greek mythology, claimed to have invented the saw and the compass. In other sources, Perdix was the name of Daedalus's sister, and her inventor son was named Talos, Kalos, or Attalus.

Q610197.label: Lyncus
Q610197.lead: In Greek mythology, King Lyncus of the Scythians was taught the arts of agriculture by Triptolemus but he refused to teach it to his people and then tried to kill Triptolemus. Demeter turned him into a lynx as punishment.

Q617753.label: Belus
Q617753.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q617753.lead: In Greek mythology, Belus was a king of Egypt and father of Aegyptus and Danaus and (usually) brother to Agenor. The wife of Belus has been named as Achiroe or Side (eponym of the Phoenician city of Sidon).

Q62109113.label: Harpyia
Q62109113.description: one of the dogs of Actaeon

Q622781.label: Asopus
Q622781.lead: Asopus or Asopos is the name of four different rivers in Greece and one in Turkey. In Greek mythology, it was also the name of the gods of those rivers.

Q622809.label: Pyrrha
Q622809.description: daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora in Greek mythology
Q622809.lead: In Greek mythology, Pyrrha is the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, or of Prometheus.

Q624551.label: Nephele
Q624551.description: cloud goddess, wife of Athamas and mother of Phrixus and Helle
Q624551.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Nephele called Nebula by Latin authors, is the name of two figures associated with clouds, who figure respectively in the stories of Ixion and in the story of Phrixus and his sister Helle.

Q633120.label: Pandrosus
Q633120.description: daughter of Cecrops I in Greek mythology
Q633120.lead: Pandrosos or Pandrosus was known in Greek myth as one of the three daughters of Cecrops I, the first king of Athens, and Aglaurus, daughter of King Actaeus.

Q633549.label: Turnus
Q633549.description: mythical character King of the Rutuli
Q633549.lead: Turnus was the legendary King of the Rutuli in Roman mythology, and the chief antagonist of the hero Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid. According to the Aeneid, Turnus is the son of Daunus and the nymph Venilia and is brother of the nymph Juturna.

Q637955.label: Neleus
Q637955.description: mythical son of Poseidon or Cretheus and father of Nestor
Q637955.lead: Neleus was a mythological king of Pylos. In some accounts, he was also counted as an Argonaut instead of his son, Nestor.

Q641065.label: Phineus
Q641065.description: son of Agenor in Greek mythology
Q641065.lead: In Greek mythology, Phineus was a king of Salmydessus in Thrace and seer, who appears in accounts of the Argonauts' voyage. Some accounts make him a king in Paphlagonia or in Arcadia.

Q641286.label: Rhodos
Q641286.description: Goddess of Rhodes in Greek mythology
Q641286.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhodos/Rhodus or Rhode (Ancient Greek: Ῥόδη, romanized: Rhódē), was the goddess and personification of the island of Rhodes and a wife of the sun god Helios.

Q643456.label: Arethusa
Q643456.description: nymph in Greek mythology who fled from the river god Alpheus
Q643456.lead: In Greek mythology, Arethusa was a nymph who fled from her home in Arcadia beneath the sea and came up as a fresh water fountain on the island of Ortygia in Syracuse, Sicily.

Q643504.label: Cephalus
Q643504.description: son of Deioneus and beloved of Eos in Greek mythology
Q643504.lead: In Greek mythology, Cephalus or Kephalos was the son of Deion, the ruler of Phocis, and Diomede.

Q645312.label: Bacchus
Q645312.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, insanity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy, and theatre. He was also known as Bacchus (Ancient Greek: Βάκχος Bacchos) by the Greeks (a name later adopted by the Romans) for a frenzy he is said to induce called baccheia.

Q653264.label: Capetus
Q653264.lead: Capetus or Capetus Silvius(Latin: Căpĕtŭs Sĭluĭŭs) was a descendant of Aeneas and one of the legendary Latin kings of Alba Longa. He was the son of Capys, and the father of Tiberinus, after whom the Tiber river was named.

Q655566.label: Ascanius
Q655566.lead: Ascanius was a legendary king of Alba Longa (traditional reign: 1176 BC to 1138 BC) and the son of the Trojan hero Aeneas and of Creusa, daughter of Priam. He is a significant figure in Roman mythology because of his family connections: as the son of the Roman ancestor-figure Aeneas (himself the son of the goddess Venus and the Trojan prince Anchises), and as a forebear of the Roman people.

Q656881.label: Tiresias
Q656881.lead: In Greek mythology, Tiresias was a blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes, famous for clairvoyance and for being transformed into a woman for seven years. He was the son of the shepherd Everes and the nymph Chariclo.

Q656887.label: Tityos
Q656887.lead: Tityos or Tityus is a giant from Greek mythology. The son of Zeus and the mortal Elara, Tityos tried to rape the goddess Leto, a former lover of Zeus and the mother of the twin gods Artemis and Apollo.

Q659594.label: Tages
Q659594.lead: Tages was claimed as a founding prophet of Etruscan religion who is known from reports by Latin authors of the late Roman Republic and Roman Empire. He revealed a cosmic view of divinity and correct methods of ascertaining divine will concerning events of public interest.

Q66016.label: Muse
Q66016.description: goddess of the inspiration of literature, science and the arts
Q66016.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, the Muses were the inspirational goddesses of literature, science, and the arts. They were considered the source of the knowledge embodied in the poetry, lyric songs, and myths that were related orally for centuries in ancient Greek culture.

Q660623.label: Numitor
Q660623.description: King of Alba Longa, son of Procas in Roman mythology
Q660623.lead: In Roman mythology, King Numitor of Alba Longa was the maternal grandfather of Rome's founder and first king, Romulus, and his twin brother Remus. He was the son of Procas, descendant of Aeneas the Trojan, and father of the twins' mother, Rhea Silvia, and Lausus.a In 794 BC Procas died and was meant to be succeeded by Numitor.

Q6612.label: Charon
Q6612.description: ferryman of Hades in Greek-Roman mythology
Q6612.lead: In Greek mythology, Charon or Kharon is the ferryman of the Greek underworld. He transports the souls of those who have been given funeral rites across the river (often called Acheron or Styx) that borders the underworld.

Q675699.label: Epaphus
Q675699.description: mythical character, son of Zeus and Io
Q675699.lead: In Greek mythology, Epaphus, also called Apis or Munantius was a son of Zeus and king of Egypt.

Q684439.label: Tarpeia
Q684439.description: Roman mythical figure, responsible for delivering the citadel to the Sabines
Q684439.lead: In Roman legend, Tarpeia, daughter of the Roman commander Spurius Tarpeius, was a Vestal Virgin who betrayed the city of Rome to the Sabines at the time of their women's abduction for what she thought would be a reward of jewelry. She was instead crushed to death by Sabine shields and her body cast from the southern Rock (Rupes Tarpeia).

Q685243.label: Nilus
Q685243.description: god of the Nile river in Greek mythology, son of Oceanus and Tethys
Q685243.lead: In Greek mythology, Nilus is one of 3,000 river gods, who represent the god of the Nile river itself. Nilus is the son of the water gods Oceanus and Tethys.

Q690613.label: Tlepolemus
Q690613.lead: In Greek mythology, Tlepolemus was the leader of the Rhodian forces in the Trojan War.

Q7198.label: Ovid
Q7198.lead: Publius Ovidius Naso, known in English as Ovid ( OV-id), was a Roman poet who lived during the reign of Augustus. He was a younger contemporary of Virgil and Horace, with whom he is often ranked as one of the three canonical poets of Latin literature.

Q725286.label: Coronis
Q725286.description: goddess from Greek mythology: princess, daughter of Phlegyas, lover of Ischys and Apollo, mother of Asclepius; killed by Apollon and Artemis
Q725286.lead: In Greek mythology, Coronis is a Thessalian princess and a lover of the god Apollo. She was the daughter of Cleophema and Phlegyas, king of the Lapiths.

Q725527.label: Calchas
Q725527.lead: Calchas is an Argive mantis, or seer, in Greek mythology. Calchas appears in the opening scenes of the Iliad and also has a long literary history after Homer.

Q726279.label: Doris
Q726279.lead: Doris, in Greek mythology, was a sea goddess. She was one of the 3,000 Oceanids, daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q729332.label: Helenus
Q729332.lead: In Greek mythology, Helenus was a gentle and clever seer. He was also a Trojan prince as the son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy, and the twin brother of the prophetess Cassandra.

Q735623.label: Inachus
Q735623.description: river deity and king of the Argolid
Q735623.lead: In Greek mythology, Inachus or Inachos was the first king of Argos. He was one of the three thousand sons of Oceanus and Tethys.

Q739359.label: Assaracus
Q739359.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q739359.lead: In Greek mythology, Assaracus was a king of Dardania.

Q74055.label: Asbolus
Q74055.lead: In Greek mythology, Asbolus was a centaur. He was a seer and Hesiod calls him an augur (oionistes οἰωνιστής) who read omens in the flight of birds.

Q741155.label: Nycteus
Q741155.lead: In Greek mythology, Nycteus was a king of Thebes. His rule began after the death of Polydorus, and ended when he was succeeded by his brother Lycus.

Q741627.label: Daphnis
Q741627.description: mythological Greek character, son of Hermes, inventor of Bucolics
Q741627.lead: In Greek mythology, Daphnis was a legendary Sicilian cowherd who was said to be the inventor of pastoral poetry. According to Diodorus the Sicilian (1st century BC), Daphnis was born in the Heraean Mountains of central Sicily.

Q742680.label: Astraea
Q742680.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Astraea, also spelled Astrea or Astria, is a daughter of Astraeus and Eos. She is the virgin goddess of justice, and is closely associated with another Greek justice goddess, Dike, the daughter of Zeus and Themis.

Q744147.label: Iole
Q744147.lead: In Greek mythology, Iole was the daughter of King Eurytus of Oechalia. According to the brief epitome in the Bibliotheca, Eurytus had a beautiful young daughter named Iole who was eligible for marriage.

Q749966.label: Oeneus
Q749966.lead: In Greek mythology, Oeneus was a Calydonian king. He was the first who received a vine-plant from Dionysos.

Q750236.label: Polyxena
Q750236.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyxena was the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy and his queen, Hecuba. She does not appear in Homer, but in several other classical authors, though the details of her story vary considerably.

Q750580.label: Pittheus
Q750580.description: son of Pelops in Greek mythology
Q750580.lead: In Greek mythology, Pittheus was the king of Troezen, city in Argolis, which he had named after his brother Troezen.

Q7559.label: dragon
Q7559.lead: A dragon is a mythical creature found in the folklore of cultures throughout the world. It is roughly serpentine in form, and often possesses features drawn from different animals, such as wings and claws.

Q771241.label: Polydectes
Q771241.lead: In Greek mythology, King Polydectes is a king of the island of Seriphos in the Cyclades. Polydectes was the ruler of the island when the Argive princess Danaë and her infant son Perseus washed ashore, having been cast away into the sea by Danaë's father Acrisius, who was afraid that his daughter's son would kill him.

Q771366.label: Myrrha
Q771366.description: daughter of Cinyras in Greek mythology
Q771366.lead: Myrrha, also known as Smyrna (Ancient Greek: Σμύρνα, romanized: Smýrna), is the mother of Adonis in Greek mythology. She was transformed into a myrrh tree after having coitus with her father, and gave birth — in tree form — to Adonis.

Q774101.label: Aura
Q774101.description: divine personification of the breeze in Greek and Roman mythology
Q774101.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Aura is a minor wind goddess, whose name means "breeze". The plural form, Aurae (Ancient Greek: Αὔραι) is sometimes found to describe a group of breeze nymphs associated with Boreas, the god of the north wind.

Q776139.label: Semele
Q776139.description: mother of Dionysus in Greek mythology
Q776139.lead: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone (Ancient Greek: Θυώνη, romanized: Thyṓnē), was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus (her own great-grandfather). Certain elements of the cult of Dionysus and Semele came from the Phrygians.

Q779406.label: Latinus
Q779406.description: king in Greek and Roman mythology
Q779406.lead: Latinus was a figure both in Greek and Roman mythology. He is often associated with the heroes of the Trojan War, namely Odysseus and Aeneas.

Q786573.label: Creon
Q786573.description: king of Corinth in Greek mythology
Q786573.lead: In Greek mythology, Creon, son of Lycaethus, was a king of Corinth and father of Hippotes and Creusa or Glauce, whom Jason would marry if not for the intervention of Medea.

Q791446.label: Battus
Q791446.lead: Battus was a figure in Greek mythology who witnessed Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle in Maenalus in Arcadia. Hermes gave him a heifer on condition Battus kept the theft secret.

Q79876.label: Isis
Q79876.lead: Isis was a major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion whose worship spread throughout the Greco-Roman world. Isis was first mentioned in the Old Kingdom as one of the main characters of the Osiris myth, in which she resurrects her slain brother and husband, the divine king Osiris, and produces and protects his heir, Horus.

Q79999.label: Uranus
Q79999.description: primordial Greek deity, god of the Sky; one of the Greek primordial deities
Q79999.lead: In Greek mythology, Uranus, sometimes written Ouranos (Ancient Greek: Οὐρανός, lit. 'sky', [uːranós]), is the personification of the sky and one of the Greek primordial deities. According to Hesiod, Uranus was the son and husband of Gaia (Earth), with whom he fathered the first generation of Titans.

Q826972.label: Beroe
Q826972.description: in Greek mythology, nurse of Semele

Q82732.label: Aeneas
Q82732.description: Trojan hero, son of Anchises and Aphrodite
Q82732.lead: Aeneas was a Trojan hero in Greco-Roman mythology, the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the Greek goddess Aphrodite (equivalent to the Roman Venus). His father was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy (both being great-grandsons of Tros, founder of Troy), making Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children (such as Hector and Paris).

Q828579.label: Salmacis
Q828579.lead: Salmacis was a naiad of Greek mythology. She rejected the ways of the virginal Greek goddess Artemis in favour of vanity and idleness.

Q83160.label: Prometheus
Q83160.description: Titan, culture hero, and trickster figure in Greek mythology who defied the gods; son of Iapetus
Q83160.lead: In Greek mythology, Prometheus is a Titan who is responsible for creating and aiding humanity in its earliest days. He defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire from them and giving it to humanity.

Q83223.label: Asclepius
Q83223.lead: Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology. He is the son of Apollo and Coronis, or Arsinoe, or of Apollo alone.

Q83496.label: Cerberus
Q83496.description: three-headed dog that guards the underworld in Greek mythology
Q83496.lead: In Greek mythology, Cerberus, often referred to as the hound of Hades, is a multi-headed dog that guards the gates of the underworld to prevent the dead from leaving. He was the offspring of the monsters Echidna and Typhon, and was usually described as having three heads, a serpent for a tail, and snakes protruding from his body.

Q836311.label: Phocus
Q836311.lead: In Greek mythology, Phocus, was a prince of Aegina and son of Aeacus and Psamathe.

Q836518.label: Euros
Q836518.description: the Greek deity representing the unlucky east wind , autumn, fall of leaves, agriculture, harvest, change , balance , comfort ,adulthood and maturity
Q836518.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Eurus is the god and personification of the east wind, although sometimes he is also said to be southeast specifically. He is one of the four principal wind gods, the Anemoi, alongside his brothers Boreas (north wind), Zephyrus (west wind) and Notus (south wind).

Q836525.label: Heliades
Q836525.description: daughters of Helios in Greek mythology
Q836525.lead: In Greek mythology, the Heliades were the daughters of Helios and Clymene, an Oceanid nymph. They were also called Phaethontides (Ancient Greek: Φαεθοντίδες, lit. 'daughters of Phaethon'), due to "Phaethon" being a common epithet for Helios.

Q836792.label: Klymene
Q836792.lead: In Greek mythology, Clymene or Klymene is the name of one of the three thousand Oceanid nymphs, usually the wife of Iapetus and mother by him of Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas and Menoetius.

Q837699.label: Evander of Pallene
Q837699.description: mythical character of Greek and Roman mythology, king of Pallantium
Q837699.lead: In Roman mythology, Evander was a culture hero from Arcadia, Greece, who was said to have brought the pantheon, laws, and alphabet of Greece to ancient Italy, where he founded the city of Pallantium on the future site of Palatine Hill, Rome, sixty years before the Trojan War. He instituted the festival of the Lupercalia.

Q846129.label: Syrinx
Q846129.description: nymph transformed into hollow water reeds in Greek mythology
Q846129.lead: In classical Greek mythology, Syrinx was an Arcadian nymph and a follower of Artemis, known for her chastity. Being pursued by Pan, she fled into the river Ladon, and at her own request was metamorphosed into a reed from which Pan then made his panpipes.

Q847268.label: Hyllus
Q847268.description: son of Heracles and Deianira in Greek mythology
Q847268.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyllus or Hyllas (Ὕλλᾱς, Hyllas) was a son of Heracles and Deianira and the husband of Iole.

Q855426.label: Byblis
Q855426.description: mythological character from Miletus, transformed into a spring
Q855426.lead: In Greek mythology, Byblis or Bublis was a daughter of Miletus. Her mother was either Tragasia, daughter of Celaenus; Cyanee, daughter of the river-god Meander; or Eidothea, daughter of King Eurytus of Caria.

Q859392.label: Ops
Q859392.description: Roman goddess of earth and fertility
Q859392.lead: In ancient Roman religion, Ops, (Latin: "Plenty") also spelled Opes or Opis, was a fertility and earth goddess of abundance, prosperity, and agriculture, and the consort of Saturn. As Ops Consiva, she presided over the reserved portion of the harvest alongside Consus, the god of stored grain.

Q860314.label: Orcus
Q860314.lead: Orcus was a god of the underworld in Roman mythology. As with Hades, the name of the god was also used for the underworld itself.

Q866674.label: Clytie
Q866674.lead: Clytie or Clytia (Ancient Greek: Κλυτία, romanized: Klutía, lit. 'renowned') is a water nymph, daughter of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys in Greek mythology. She is thus one of the 3,000 Oceanid nymphs, and sister to the 3,000 river-gods.

Q8667.label: Boötes
Q8667.description: constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere
Q8667.lead: Boötes ( boh-OH-teez) is a constellation in the northern sky, located between 0° and +60° declination, and 13 and 16 hours of right ascension on the celestial sphere. The name comes from Latin: Boōtēs, which comes from Ancient Greek: Βοώτης, romanized: Boṓtēs 'herdsman' or 'plowman'.

Q878246.label: Cinyras
Q878246.description: mythical founder of the city of Paphos in Greek mythology
Q878246.lead: In Greek mythology, Cinyras was a famous hero and king of Cyprus. Accounts vary significantly as to his genealogy and provide a variety of stories concerning him; in many sources he is associated with the cult of Aphrodite on Cyprus, and Adonis, a consort of Aphrodite, is mentioned as his son.

Q887384.label: Procas
Q887384.lead: Procas Sylvius or Proca was one of the Latin kings of Alba Longa in the mythic tradition of the founding of Rome. He was the father of Amulius and Numitor and the great-grandfather of Romulus and Remus, Rome's legendary founders.

Q889656.label: Amulius
Q889656.description: mythical king of Alba Longa who ordered the death of Romulus and Remus
Q889656.lead: In Roman mythology, Amulius was king of Alba Longa who ordered the death of his infant, twin grandnephews Romulus, the eventual founder and king of Rome, and Remus. He was deposed and killed by them after they survived and grew to adulthood.

Q905162.label: Dido
Q905162.description: legendary founder and first queen of Carthage
Q905162.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Dido, also known as Elissa ( il-ISS-ə; Greek: Ἔλισσα), was the legendary founder and first queen of the Phoenician city-state of Carthage. In most accounts, she was originally the joint ruler of Tyre who fled tyranny to found her own city in northwest Africa, now modern-day Tunisia.

Q910403.label: Dryope
Q910403.description: daughter of Dryops, Eyrypylus, or Eurytus, mother of Amphissus
Q910403.lead: In Greek mythology, Dryope is the daughter of Dryops, king of Oeta ("oak-man") or of Eurytus (and hence half-sister to Iole). Dryope mothered Amphissus by Apollo.

Q911084.label: Alpheus
Q911084.description: river and river god in Greek mythology
Q911084.lead: In Greek mythology, Alpheus or Alpheios was the river god who embodied the river of the same name.

Q9147465.label: Alphenor
Q9147465.description: son of Amphion in Greek mythology
Q9147465.lead: Archenor or Acheinor was in Greek mythology one of the Niobids, and perhaps the same who is called by Ovid "Alphenor". The names of the Niobids, however, differ very much in the different lists.

Q922330.label: Lichas
Q922330.lead: In Greek mythology, Lichas was Heracles' servant, who brought the poisoned shirt from Deianira to Hercules because of Deianira's jealousy of Iole, which killed him.

Q93172.label: Gaia
Q93172.description: Greek primordial deity, the personification of the Earth
Q93172.lead: In Greek mythology, Gaia, also spelled Gaea, is the personification of Earth. She is the mother of Uranus (Sky), with whom she conceived the Titans (themselves parents of many of the Olympian gods), the Cyclopes, and the Giants, as well as of Pontus (Sea), from whose union she bore the primordial sea gods.

Q9338656.label: Smilax
Q9338656.lead: In Greek mythology Smilax was the lover of Crocus and was turned into the plant bearing her name (the bindweed). Ancient sources with information about her and her tale are few and far between.

Q935433.label: Elpenor
Q935433.lead: Elpenor was the youngest comrade of Odysseus in Greek mythology. While on the island of Circe, he became drunk and decided to spend the night on the roof.

Q936486.label: Phantasos
Q936486.lead: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Phantasos is one of the thousand sons of Somnus (Sleep, the Roman counterpart of Hypnos). He appeared in dreams in the form of inanimate objects, putting on "deceptive shapes of earth, rocks, water, trees, all lifeless things".

Q937512.label: Tiberinus
Q937512.lead: Tiberinus is a figure in Roman mythology. He was the god of the Tiber River.

Q939149.label: Eurytus
Q939149.lead: Eurytus of Oechalia (Οἰχαλίᾱ, Oikhalíā), Thessaly, was a skillful archer of Greek mythology who was even said to have instructed Heracles in the art of using the bow.

Q94072.label: Autonoë
Q94072.lead: In Greek mythology, Autonoë was a Theban princess as the eldest daughter of Cadmus, founder of Thebes in Boeotia, and the goddess Harmonia. She was the wife of Aristaeus and mother of Actaeon and possibly Macris.

Q949290.label: Enipeus
Q949290.lead: Enipeus, in ancient Greece, was a river god. Enipeus was loved by a mortal woman named Tyro, who was married to a mortal man named Cretheus.

Q960039.label: Titus Tatius
Q960039.lead: According to the Roman foundation myth, Titus Tatius, also called Tatius Sabinus, was king of the Sabines from Cures and joint-ruler of the Kingdom of Rome for several years. During the reign of Romulus, the first king of Rome, Tatius declared war on Rome in response to the incident known as the rape of the Sabine Women.

Q969168.label: Plexippus
Q969168.description: son of Thestius in Greek mythology

Q972143.label: Oedipus
Q972143.lead: Oedipus is a fabula crepidata (Roman tragic play with Greek subject) of c. 1061 lines of verse that was written by Lucius Annaeus Seneca at some time during the 1st century AD. It is a retelling of the story of Oedipus, which is better known through the play Oedipus Rex by the Athenian playwright, Sophocles.

Q993387.label: Eurylochus
Q993387.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurylochus appears in Homer's Odyssey as second-in-command of Odysseus' ship during the return to Ithaca after the Trojan War. He is portrayed as an unpleasant, cowardly individual who undermines Odysseus and stirs up trouble.
